The answer is the Sun. As a comet's orbit brings it closer to the Sun, the Sun's heat warms its surface. Frozen gases turn directly into gas, and as they escape, they carry dust with them. This material forms a huge, cloudy shell around the solid centre, called the coma. From the coma, most comets grow not one tail but two.

The dust tail consists of tiny solid grains released from the comet. Sunlight pushes on them through radiation pressure, while gravity and their existing motion also affect their paths. The resulting tail often forms a broad curve. It appears white or yellow because the dust reflects sunlight.

The ion tail forms from gas that becomes electrically charged, for example when ultraviolet light removes electrons. Interactions with the solar wind and its magnetic field carry these ions away from the Sun. The solar wind is a fast stream of charged particles flowing outward from the Sun. Ion tails are often narrow, relatively straight, and blue.

The main tails generally extend away from the Sun, rather than simply following behind the comet. After a comet passes its closest point and moves outward, its tails can stretch ahead of it. Viewing angle and dust distribution can also produce apparent exceptions to the usual direction.

Comet tails even helped scientists discover the solar wind. In 1951, the astronomer Ludwig Biermann noticed that ion tails pointed in directions that sunlight alone could not explain. He argued that a steady flow of particles from the Sun must be pushing them. Later, spacecraft confirmed that this solar wind is real.

The interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS, discovered in July 2025, offered a comparison with comets from our solar system. Early observations showed a short feature apparently pointing towards the Sun. Researchers considered how dust released from the sunlit side and viewing geometry might explain it. Later images showed a more usual dust tail extending away from the Sun. By late November, photographs showed a green coma, a faint blue ion tail bent by the solar wind, and a small sunward feature. The comet passed closest to the Sun in late October and closest to Earth in mid-December before continuing outward. These features gave researchers ways to compare its behaviour with that of other comets.

passages.title: How Good Are Crows at Maths?
paragraphs: Crows have a reputation as some of the cleverest birds on Earth. Some can even make simple tools. In recent years, a laboratory at the University of Tübingen in Germany has been asking a more surprising question: how much do crows understand about numbers and shapes?

The lab, led by the neuroscientist Andreas Nieder, trains carrion crows to play games on a touchscreen. In one study published in the journal Science in 2024, a team led by Diana Liao tested whether crows could count out loud. Very young children often do something similar before they learn number words. They produce the same number of sounds as the objects they see, such as three claps for three toys.

The researchers trained three crows over more than a year, in more than 160 sessions. On the screen, they showed a number from 1 to 4, or played a sound linked to one of those numbers. The crow then had to produce the same number of caws within about ten seconds, and then peck an "enter" key on the screen to show it had finished. A correct answer earned a reward, such as a mealworm.

The crows generally performed well. For larger numbers, they paused longer before answering and made more mistakes, a pattern also seen in young children learning to count. Features of the first caw varied with the total number of caws that followed. This suggested that each crow planned the whole sequence before it started, rather than simply calling until it happened to stop. The finding supports an ability to control the number of calls in this trained task.

In April 2025, the lab published a study in which two trained crows had to select the odd shape from a set of six. After practice with clearly different shapes, they received more similar sets, such as five squares and one slightly distorted four-sided figure. They performed best when the regular shapes had features such as right angles, parallel sides, or symmetry. Their success also extended to trials without rewards. This suggests sensitivity to geometric regularity under the conditions tested; it does not establish that every crow would succeed without training.

Both studies used small samples: three crows for counting and two for shapes. The birds had extensive laboratory training, so the results cannot yet show how widely these abilities occur among wild crows. Researchers propose that sensitivity to shape could help with feeding or navigation, but those uses still need to be tested.

passages.title: Is South Korea’s Fertility Rate Recovering?
paragraphs: South Korea’s total fertility rate fell from 1.24 in 2015 to 0.72 in 2023. This measure estimates the number of children a woman would have if the age-specific birth rates observed in a given year continued throughout her childbearing years. It differs from simply counting births or dividing births by the whole population.

Then the numbers started to move the other way. In 2024, the rate rose to 0.75, the first increase in nine years. In 2025, according to preliminary government data, it rose again to 0.80. In 2024, about 238,300 babies were born, up 3.6 percent from a record low of about 230,000 the year before. Births in 2025 grew by another 6.8 percent, the biggest yearly jump since 2007. News reports described a rebound, and some asked whether the country had finally turned a corner.

Several factors may help explain the rise. Marriages increased by 14.9 percent in 2024 and rose again in 2025. Many couples had postponed their weddings during the COVID-19 pandemic and married later. A relatively large group of women was also entering its early to mid thirties. Government support included cash grants, parental leave, childcare, and housing assistance. These changes offer possible explanations, but their separate effects cannot be established from the headline figures alone.

The scale of recovery depends on the comparison. A rate of 0.80 is above 0.72, but still below 1.24 in 2015 and less than half the replacement level of about 2.1. Replacement fertility concerns replacing generations over the long term; it does not guarantee immediate population stability, which also depends on age structure and migration. Seoul’s rate was 0.63 in 2025, despite increasing from the previous year.

Some influences may be temporary. A surge in weddings previously delayed by the pandemic cannot continue indefinitely. Smaller groups of women will also follow the relatively large group now in its thirties, potentially limiting the number of births. Changes in age composition affect birth counts, while the timing of childbearing can affect a year’s fertility rate. These different measures need to be examined separately.

The government forecast cited in the report projects a fertility rate above 1.0 by 2031. That is a projection, not an established outcome. Whether the increase lasts will depend on future decisions about marriage and childbearing as well as the conditions shaping those decisions.

passages.title: Do School Phone Bans Work?
paragraphs: Many parents and teachers worry that smartphones harm young people's sleep, focus, and mental health. As a result, a growing number of schools and governments have decided to restrict phones during the school day. In February 2024, the UK government published guidance asking schools in England to ban phone use for the whole day, including breaks. The guidance is not compulsory, but it sent a strong signal. The big question is simple: do these bans actually help?

In February 2025, a team led by Victoria Goodyear at the University of Birmingham published what it called the first study of its kind. The researchers collected data from 1,227 students aged 12 to 15 in 30 secondary schools in England. Twenty of the schools had restrictive rules, where phones were usually switched off and kept in bags. The other ten allowed some phone use during the day. The team then compared the students in both groups. The study was funded by the UK's National Institute for Health and Care Research. Before starting, the team had searched for earlier research and found no published, peer-reviewed study that had tested whether school phone rules improve students' mental health.

The study did not find evidence of better mental wellbeing, sleep, physical activity, or exam results among students in schools with stricter rules. Overall phone use was not lower either. Students in those schools reported less use during school hours but more use outside them. This comparison does not establish that the rules caused students to shift their use to other times.

Across the sample, greater phone and social media use was associated with poorer mental wellbeing, less sleep, lower grades, and more disruptive classroom behaviour. These associations do not by themselves establish causation. Goodyear argued that reducing overall use was an important goal and that school rules alone might be insufficient.

Not everyone accepts the study's conclusion. Supporters of phone bans have pointed out several weaknesses. The study took a snapshot at one moment in time, so it could compare the two groups of schools but could not prove what caused any differences. Because it was an observational study, the schools had chosen their own rules, and the schools that chose bans might have been different in other ways. Critics also noted that earlier studies had found some benefits from bans.

Other researchers say the details of each ban matter. A study in the Netherlands, which collected data from 27 secondary schools between September 2024 and February 2025, looked at how different types of bans affect students' sense of connection at school. Its authors noted that the English study had found no differences between different types of bans either. They argued that research should look at how strict and how wide a ban is, not only at whether a school has one.

The Birmingham study raises doubts about whether school bans alone reduce total phone use or improve wellbeing. Its observational design also limits what can be concluded about causes. Evaluating a ban requires attention to its rules, implementation, and the students’ circumstances.

passages.title: Why Is Arctic Sea Ice Shrinking Even in Winter?
paragraphs: Most news about melting Arctic ice focuses on summer, when the ice shrinks to its smallest size. But in March 2025, scientists reported something worrying about winter. On 22 March, the sea ice covering the Arctic Ocean reached its largest size of the year, known as the annual maximum. Yet even at its biggest, the ice covered less area than in any winter since satellite records began in 1979.

Sea ice is frozen seawater that floats on the ocean. In the Arctic, it grows during the cold, dark winter and melts during the summer. Scientists measure it using satellites, and they usually describe its size as its extent. This means the area of ocean where at least some ice is present. Every year, the extent rises to a maximum around March and falls to a minimum around September.

According to the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC) at the University of Colorado Boulder, the 2025 maximum extent was 14.33 million square kilometres. This was 80,000 square kilometres below the previous record low, set in 2017. It was also 1.31 million square kilometres below the average maximum for 1981 to 2010. The maximum also came about ten days later than the average date of 12 March. The date changes from year to year. It has come as early as 24 February and as late as 2 April.

The ice was low across most of the Arctic during the winter of 2024 to 2025. The Gulf of St. Lawrence in Canada stayed almost free of ice, and the Sea of Okhotsk near Russia had much less ice than normal. Only the East Greenland Sea was close to average. In the Bering Sea, near Alaska, the ice stayed low for most of the season, but it grew quickly from late February, which helps explain why the maximum came late. Across the Arctic as a whole, the ice had been at or near record lows since December. One possible reason, according to reports on the data, is that air temperatures around the Arctic Ocean were 1 to 2 degrees Celsius higher than average, which may have slowed the growth of new ice.

The record is part of a long pattern. All ten of the smallest winter maximums in the satellite record have happened since 2007. Before 2005, a maximum below 15 million square kilometres had never been recorded. Since then, it has happened many times. Walt Meier, a senior scientist at NSIDC, said that the new record shows how Arctic ice has fundamentally changed from earlier decades. He added that the most important point is not the single record, but the continuing long-term loss of ice in all seasons.

The Arctic record was also part of a wider picture. Around the same time, sea ice around Antarctica reached one of its lowest summer minimums on record. Some scientists warn that the Arctic could have summers with almost no sea ice by around 2035.

NSIDC stressed that such figures are first announced as preliminary and checked again later. Even so, year after year, the same direction appears in the data: less ice, in winter as well as in summer.

passages.title: What Happens When a Computer Stops Getting Updates?
paragraphs: On 14 October 2025, Microsoft officially ended support for Windows 10, the operating system that had run on hundreds of millions of computers for a decade. At that time, around 60 percent of PCs worldwide were still using it. Many people worried that their computers would suddenly stop working. They did not. But something important did change.

An operating system is the main software that controls a computer. Like any large program, it contains mistakes. Some of these mistakes are security weaknesses that criminals can use to break in, steal information, or install harmful programs. When a company discovers such a weakness, it releases a patch, a small piece of software that fixes the problem. For years, Windows 10 received these security patches regularly.

End of standard support means that regular security patches stopped. Without extended support or another supported system, new weaknesses may remain unpatched. Microsoft also stopped providing standard bug fixes and technical help. As a result, a computer running an unsupported copy of Windows 10 becomes more vulnerable over time. Antivirus programs can help, but they cannot fully replace system patches. Some apps may eventually stop working properly on the old system.

Why would Microsoft end support at all? Windows versions normally follow a life cycle of about ten years, and Windows 10 was first released in 2015. Interestingly, Windows 10 was not originally expected to have a separate successor. Microsoft had suggested it would simply keep improving through updates, so the arrival of Windows 11 six years later surprised many users. Microsoft wanted users to migrate to Windows 11. However, Windows 11 has stricter hardware requirements, including a security chip called TPM 2.0, so many older computers cannot upgrade. Microsoft offers a free tool called PC Health Check, which tells users whether their computer meets the requirements.

For people who were not ready, Microsoft offered a temporary option called Extended Security Updates, or ESU. Home users could pay about 30 dollars for one extra year of critical security updates, lasting until 13 October 2026. Some users could get it free by syncing their files to Microsoft's cloud storage. To join, a computer needed the latest version of Windows 10, the most recent updates, and a Microsoft account. Businesses could pay for up to three years, but the price doubled each year, from 61 dollars to 122 dollars and then 244 dollars per device. This was designed to encourage them to upgrade sooner. Schools received a much cheaper offer.

People had several choices. They could upgrade to Windows 11 if their computer was able to, buy a new computer, pay for ESU, or switch to a different system such as Linux or ChromeOS. Experts also suggested that anyone keeping an unsupported computer should avoid risky activities on it, such as online banking.

The lesson goes beyond Windows. Phones, tablets, and even smart home devices also eventually stop receiving updates. A device can keep working perfectly well while slowly becoming less safe. Knowing when support ends is an important part of using technology wisely.

passages.title: The Baby Who Received His Own Gene Treatment
paragraphs: When KJ Muldoon was only a week old, doctors in Philadelphia gave his parents terrible news. He had a very rare genetic disease called severe CPS1 deficiency, which affects roughly one in a million babies. About half of infants with this condition die within the first week of life. KJ was given perhaps six months to live.

CPS1 deficiency is caused by a single mistake in the DNA. The human genome contains about three billion letters, and in KJ's case, one wrong letter in a gene called CPS1 stopped his body from making an important enzyme. Without this enzyme, the liver cannot remove ammonia, a waste product that forms when the body breaks down protein. The ammonia builds up in the blood and becomes toxic, damaging the brain and other organs. Normally, patients must follow a very strict diet and, when they are old enough, may need a liver transplant.

KJ's doctors, Rebecca Ahrens-Nicklas at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and Kiran Musunuru at Penn Medicine, had been working on gene-editing treatments for this group of liver diseases since 2023. That preparation allowed them to do something never done before. In about six months, they designed a treatment tailored to KJ's exact genetic mistake.

The treatment used a type of CRISPR technology called base editing. Instead of cutting DNA, a base editor finds one wrong letter and changes it to the correct one. CRISPR, the tool behind this technology, won its inventors the Nobel Prize in 2020. In KJ's case, the treatment was designed to correct one of his two copies of the CPS1 gene. To reach the liver, the editing tools were packed inside tiny fat particles called lipid nanoparticles. As Ahrens-Nicklas explained, the drug was designed only for KJ, because the genetic changes it targets were specific to him.

KJ received his first dose in February 2025, when he was about six to seven months old, followed by further doses in March and April. There were no serious complications. Afterwards, he was able to eat more protein, and his weight rose from below the 10th percentile to above the 35th. In May 2025, the team described his case in the New England Journal of Medicine, and Musunuru presented it at a major meeting of gene therapy experts in New Orleans. Later that year, after 307 days in the hospital, KJ went home with his parents, Nicole and Kyle, accompanied by a police escort.

The doctors are careful about what they claim. KJ is only one patient, and it is too early to know how well the treatment will work in the long term. However, the case shows that a gene-editing treatment can be designed and approved for a single patient in months rather than years.

According to the hospital, the method could open new possibilities for patients with rare conditions that currently have no available treatments. Musunuru hopes KJ's case can become a model for creating personalised treatments quickly for other patients with their own unique mutations. As Ahrens-Nicklas put it, KJ is just one patient, but the team hopes he is the first of many.

passages.title: How Did Japan Choose Its First Woman Prime Minister?
paragraphs: On 21 October 2025, the members of Japan's parliament stood and applauded as the results were announced. Sanae Takaichi had become the first woman to lead the country as prime minister. As the numbers were read out, she stood up and bowed deeply.

In many countries, people vote directly for their leader. Japan works differently. It is a parliamentary system, so the prime minister is chosen by parliament, known as the Diet. The Diet has two houses, and the lower house, called the House of Representatives, has the final say. In practice, the prime minister is usually the leader of the largest party or group of parties.

For most of the past several decades, the largest party has been the Liberal Democratic Party, or LDP. So the road to becoming prime minister often begins inside the LDP. In September 2025, Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba announced he would step down after his party suffered heavy losses in elections in 2024 and in July 2025. The LDP then held a leadership election with five candidates, voted on by both party members and party lawmakers. Takaichi, who had strong support from ordinary members, won the final round against Shinjiro Koizumi and became party leader on 4 October.

However, becoming party leader was not enough. Just days later, the LDP's long-time partner, a centrist party called Komeito, left the governing coalition. Komeito, which is backed by a Buddhist organisation, is known for its more moderate views. Its departure threatened the LDP, which had governed Japan almost without interruption for decades. Without Komeito, the LDP no longer had enough seats to be sure of winning the vote in parliament. Takaichi quickly formed a new coalition with the Japan Innovation Party, known as Ishin no Kai, which is based in Osaka. The two parties signed an agreement on 20 October, just one day before the vote. They promised to cooperate on the economy, public finances, foreign affairs, national security, and energy. However, the Japan Innovation Party said it would not take any positions in the cabinet until it felt more confident about the partnership.

In the lower house, Takaichi won 237 votes, four more than the 233 needed for a majority. Her main rival, Yoshihiko Noda of the Constitutional Democratic Party, received 149 votes. One reason she won was that the opposition parties failed to unite behind a single candidate. In the upper house, she won with 125 votes, just one more than required. She then formally took office after an appointment ceremony with the Emperor, and formed a cabinet that included several of her former rivals.

Takaichi is known as a conservative politician and was a close ally of former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe. Her election was historic, but her position was not secure. Her new coalition was still short of a majority in both houses of parliament, so her government would need support from other parties to pass laws. Analysts warned that this could make her government unstable. Her party said its first priority would be dealing with rising prices.
Japan's experience shows that in a parliamentary system, winning power depends not only on popularity, but also on building and keeping partnerships in parliament.

passages.title: Why Did America Stop Making Pennies?
paragraphs: On 12 November 2025, at the United States Mint in Philadelphia, workers pressed the final one-cent coin, or penny, for circulation. The penny had been produced for more than 230 years. The Mint also planned to auction 232 special sets of final pennies for collectors, each including one made of gold. The coin had been authorised by the Coinage Act of 1792 and became part of everyday language, in sayings such as a penny saved is a penny earned. The reason for ending it was simple: making a penny had become much more expensive than the coin was worth.

The US Mint is the government agency that makes the country's coins. When the Mint makes a coin, it usually earns a small profit, because the coin's face value is higher than the cost of producing it. Economists call this profit seigniorage. For the penny, however, the opposite was true. According to the Mint's 2024 annual report, each penny cost about 3.69 cents to make and distribute, mainly because of the cost of the metals. With more than three billion pennies distributed that year, the Mint lost about 85.3 million dollars on them.

In February 2025, President Donald Trump directed the Treasury to stop producing new pennies, calling them wasteful. The Treasury said stopping production could save about 56 million dollars a year in material costs. It also pointed out that people were using pennies much less, as more payments are made by card or phone.

Ending production does not mean pennies disappear overnight. More than 114 billion pennies are still in circulation, and they remain legal to use. However, as the supply slowly shrinks, shops will increasingly need to round cash payments to the nearest five cents. A total of 1.02 dollars, for example, might become 1.00 dollar, while 1.03 dollars might become 1.05 dollars. Card and digital payments can still be charged to the exact cent. Some experts expect the effect on prices to be very small, with some going up and others going down.
Other countries have already done this. Canada and Australia, for example, stopped using their lowest-value coins years ago, and a study of Canadian grocery prices examined how rounding worked there.

Yet the penny decision has raised new questions. The nickel, the five-cent coin, loses even more cents per coin, costing about 13.78 cents each. As pennies disappear, people may need more nickels, which could increase costs rather than reduce them. The Mint said it was watching the situation. By contrast, the Mint earns a profit on dimes and quarters. A dime costs about 5.76 cents to make, and a quarter about 14.68 cents. According to Axios, a government report warned that also eliminating the nickel could cost consumers up to 56 million dollars a year through rounding.

Inflation also helps explain why the penny became less useful. As the general level of prices rises, a single cent buys less, while the costs of materials and coin production can increase. The end of the penny shows how money itself must change as the economy changes. A coin that served Americans for centuries became too costly to keep, but replacing it creates new challenges of its own.

passages.title: How Will the World's Biggest Hydropower Project Work?
paragraphs: On 19 July 2025, Chinese Premier Li Qiang attended a ceremony in Nyingchi, a city in Tibet near the border with India. He announced the start of construction on a huge hydropower project on the Yarlung Tsangpo River. When it is finished, it is expected to become the largest hydropower facility in the world.

Hydropower means making electricity from moving water. The basic idea is simple. Water flowing downhill has energy. When it is guided through a turbine, the moving water spins the blades, and a generator connected to the turbine turns that motion into electricity. The more water there is, and the further it falls, the more electricity can be produced.

This is why the location of the new project matters so much. The Yarlung Tsangpo flows through the Tibetan Plateau and then makes a sharp turn called the Great Bend. There, the river passes through what is described as the world's deepest gorge, a narrow valley with steep sides. In a short distance, the river drops by around 2,000 metres. That enormous fall gives the water a great deal of energy.

The project, often called the Medog Hydropower Station, is planned as a series of five cascade power stations along the river. Its planned capacity is 60,000 megawatts. It is expected to produce about 300 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity each year, roughly three times as much as the Three Gorges Dam, which is currently the world's largest hydropower station. According to one report, that is enough to meet the needs of about 300 million people. Most of the electricity is expected to be sent to other regions of China, while some will be used locally in Tibet.

The project is also one of the most expensive in the world. Reported costs range from about 1 trillion yuan, or 137 billion dollars, to 1.2 trillion yuan, or about 167 billion dollars. It is being built by a new state company, China Yajiang Group, and commercial operation is planned for around 2033.

However, the river does not stay in China. After leaving Tibet, it flows into India, where it is called the Brahmaputra, and then into Bangladesh, where it is known as the Jamuna. Many millions of people live downstream. Both India and Bangladesh have expressed concern about possible effects on water supply, farming, and the environment. According to one analysis, the main worry is not the total amount of water each year, which depends on the monsoon, but when and how water is released. Bangladesh formally asked China for detailed environmental and disaster studies, and Chinese officials told Bangladesh that the project would not divert water from the river. In India, leaders in the border state of Arunachal Pradesh described the project as a serious threat, and the Indian government has asked Beijing several times to respect India's interests. The new project also follows a chain of smaller dams that China has already built on the same river since 2015.

China has said the project has been carefully studied and will not harm people or ecosystems downstream. It has also said it will keep communicating with neighbouring countries. As construction continues, the project shows how a single engineering plan on one river can affect several countries at once.

passages.title: Did Astronomers Just Find a New Dwarf Planet?
paragraphs: In May 2025, a team of astronomers announced the discovery of a distant object in our solar system with a rather dull name: 2017 OF201. Behind that name is an exciting possibility. The object may be a new dwarf planet, and its unusual path around the Sun could change a long debate about a hidden planet.

The team was led by Sihao Cheng of the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, working with Jiaxuan Li and Eritas Yang of Princeton University. They did not use a new telescope. Instead, they searched through existing images from earlier sky surveys, using careful methods to track the faint moving object. The discovery was officially announced by the International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center on 21 May 2025. The team found the object in 19 images taken over seven years, and later reported 24 observations over about 20 years, which allowed them to calculate its orbit precisely.

The object is currently about 90 times farther from the Sun than the Earth is. Its orbit is extremely stretched. At its closest, it is about 45 times the Earth-Sun distance, which is still well beyond Neptune. At its farthest, it travels more than 1,600 times the Earth-Sun distance, reaching into the icy region known as the Oort cloud. One trip around the Sun takes about 25,000 years. Its path goes so far out that, according to Cheng, it may once have passed close to stars other than our Sun. Because it is so far away most of the time, it can be observed from Earth for only about one percent of each orbit.

Why do astronomers call it a candidate rather than a confirmed dwarf planet? Its size was not measured directly. Assuming the object reflects a typical amount of sunlight, the team estimated its diameter at about 700 kilometres, roughly a third the size of Pluto. That would probably be large enough for its gravity to pull it into a round shape, which is one of the conditions for being a dwarf planet. Cheng's team is looking for more data to confirm it.

The discovery also affects the search for Planet Nine. Some astronomers have suggested that a large, unseen planet, about five to ten times the mass of the Earth, may exist far beyond Neptune. Their main evidence is that several distant objects have orbits that seem to point in similar directions, as if something is shepherding them. But 2017 OF201 is an outlier. Its orbit points in a very different direction from that cluster.

According to Li, this could potentially challenge the Planet Nine idea. However, other researchers noted that the study tested only one possible orbit for Planet Nine. Scientists will need many more distant objects to decide.

More than 5,000 objects beyond Neptune have already been found, but few are as large or travel as far. Cheng believes there may be around a hundred similar objects that are simply too far away to see for now. The outer solar system, once thought to be almost empty, may be much busier than expected.

passages.title: Why Do Humpback Whales Blow Rings at People?
paragraphs: Imagine being on a small boat when a huge humpback whale swims slowly towards you, rolls in the water, and then releases a perfect ring of bubbles, like a person blowing a smoke ring. For a small number of lucky people, this really happened. In 2025, scientists studied these moments for the first time.

Humpback whales are already known to use bubbles in clever ways. When hunting, groups of whales can blow bubble nets around small fish, trapping them before feeding. Males also produce trails and bursts of bubbles when competing for a female. But the rings in the new study seemed different. They were not connected to feeding or competition.

The research was carried out by scientists from the SETI Institute and the University of California, Davis, and published in the journal Marine Mammal Science in May 2025. The team collected reports, photos, and videos from naturalists, researchers, and citizen scientists. Altogether, they analysed 12 episodes, involving 39 bubble rings made by 11 different whales, in places including Hawaii, the Dominican Republic, and the Atlantic coast of the United States.

In most cases, the whales seemed calm and curious. They often approached boats or swimmers slowly, sometimes coming within one body length, before blowing a ring. In ten of the twelve episodes, the rings were made near people. The researchers also checked hundreds of hours of drone footage of whales from other studies, recorded when no humans were nearby. They found no examples of these rings. According to Josephine Hubbard, one of the authors, the contrast raises the possibility that human presence is connected with the behaviour, though it does not establish that the rings occur only near people.

What do the rings mean? The scientists are careful not to claim too much. They point out that humpbacks live in complex societies, make a wide variety of sounds, and have even been seen helping other species attacked by predators. As the animal expert Karen Pryor once noted, patterns of bubbles give whales and dolphins a way of communicating that land mammals simply do not have. Co-lead author Fred Sharpe suggested that the whales may be trying to play, watch how people react, or communicate in some way. Laurance Doyle of the SETI Institute compared it to a dog putting a ball in front of you to invite you to play. One well-known female humpback called Watchtower was filmed blowing a ring beside a boat off Maui, while excited passengers cheered.

There is a surprising reason why the SETI Institute, which searches for signs of intelligent life beyond Earth, is interested in whales. Its WhaleSETI project studies how intelligent animals on Earth communicate, to help scientists recognise possible signals from space. Doyle explained that the search for alien intelligence assumes other beings might be interested in contacting humans. In his view, the curious behaviour of humpback whales supports the idea that such interest can develop naturally.
One detail showed how skilful the whales are. Frame-by-frame video analysis revealed at least one whale making a ring with only one of its two blowholes.

passages.title: What Do English Rankings Really Tell Us?
paragraphs: Each year, one international ranking of English skills attracts a lot of attention. In the 2025 edition of the EF English Proficiency Index, published by the education company EF Education First, Indonesia ranked 80th out of 123 countries and regions, with a score of 471. The global average was 488. The Netherlands was first again. The index, first published in 2011, tries to measure English proficiency, or how well adults can use the language. It groups countries into five levels, from very high, for scores of 600 and above, to very low, for scores below 450. With 471 points, Indonesia sits in the low group. Rankings like this are useful, but they are also easy to misunderstand. To read them wisely, we need to know how they are made.

The index is based on a free online test called the EF SET, which measures reading, listening, speaking, and writing. The 2025 edition used results from more than 2.2 million people who took the test in 2024. A country needed at least 400 test takers to be included. In 2024, 46 percent of test takers completed the test on a mobile phone. The most important detail is who takes the test. According to EF itself, the test takers are self-selected. People take it because they want to learn English or are curious about their level. This means the group is not guaranteed to be representative of the whole population. Almost all test takers are working adults or young adults finishing their studies. People without internet access are automatically left out. EF explains that this could make scores higher than those of the general population in places where internet use is low, because poorer and less educated people are less likely to take part.

EF also reports that its scores follow similar national trends to other tests. For example, they correlate strongly with results from TOEFL iBT, and to a lesser degree with results from the IELTS Academic test. So the index can show broad patterns, even if it is not a perfect picture.

The Indonesian results include interesting details. Scores differ by skill: reading was highest at 491, followed by writing at 479 and listening at 454, while speaking was lowest at 447. They also differ by place. Among regions, Java scored 493, while Maluku scored 416. City scores range from 523 in Jakarta to 409 in Probolinggo. They even differ by job. People working in research and development scored 556, teachers scored 479, and students scored 443.

It is tempting to draw quick conclusions from these numbers, for example, that students are worse at English than researchers because of poor teaching. But the groups are not the same. Researchers may use English every day at work, and the people who choose to take the test in each group may be very different. Comparing groups fairly requires knowing who was tested.

For teachers and learners, the index is best used as a starting point for questions, not a final judgement. It can show where gaps may exist, such as between regions or between skills. Deeper answers need classroom evidence, national tests, and careful research.
The study is based on a small number of observations, so there is still much to learn. But it offers a rare glimpse of a giant animal that seems just as curious about us as we are about it.

passages.title: Why Are Run Clubs Suddenly Everywhere?
paragraphs: On weekend mornings and weekday evenings in many cities, groups of people in bright trainers gather at a park or café, run a few kilometres together, and then stay to talk. Run clubs are not new, but they have become a global craze. One Indonesian city, South Jakarta, even appeared at the top of an international list.

The clearest evidence comes from Strava, an app that people use to record their exercise. Strava has more than 135 million users in over 190 countries. Its 2024 Year in Sport report, which combined activity data with a survey of more than 5,000 active people, found a 59 percent increase in running club participation around the world. Group runs of ten or more people rose by 18 percent, and walking clubs grew as well.

Why is this happening? The report suggests the main reason is social. More than half of the people surveyed said they had made new friends through fitness groups. Among Gen Z users, the figure was 66 percent, and 55 percent said social connection was their main reason for joining a group. Nearly one in five Gen Z respondents had gone on a date with someone they met through exercise. People were also four times more likely to prefer meeting new friends in a fitness group than in a bar.

Interest has been growing for years. Searches for the phrase run club on Google have risen over the last five years. A survey by the media company LADbible found that 72 percent of Gen Z members who go to run clubs do so to meet new people. Some writers link the trend to loneliness. For young people who spend much of their time online, a run club can offer a regular opportunity to meet others face to face.

Running together seems to help people exercise more, too. According to the report, group activities lasted about 40 percent longer than solo ones. Many runners said they joined groups to improve their performance, and about a third said the group helped them stick to their training plans. A Strava representative also suggested that, after the COVID-19 pandemic, people began paying more attention to mental health and a more balanced approach to fitness.

The report also showed how social running is in some places. Some clubs have become very large. The Mikkeller Running Club, started in Copenhagen in 2014, is said to have more than 30,000 participants in over 200 clubs around the world. Strava's report listed cities with the highest share of runs recorded together with other people. South Jakarta came first, with 78 percent, ahead of cities such as Fortaleza in Brazil, Leeds in England, and New York.

It is worth remembering that these figures come mostly from Strava users and a survey, so they describe active people rather than everyone. Still, the message is clear. For a growing number of people, running is no longer only about fitness. It is also a way to find friends and a sense of community.

passages.title: What Caused a Glacier to Bury a Swiss Village?
paragraphs: At about 3:30 in the afternoon on 28 May 2025, a huge part of the Birch Glacier broke away from a mountainside above the village of Blatten in the Swiss Alps. Ice, rock, and mud rushed down the slope. About 90 percent of the village was buried under a mass of debris around two kilometres long. The event was so powerful that it was recorded as a small earthquake, with a magnitude of 3.1. The Birch Glacier lies about 50 kilometres north of the Matterhorn, one of the most famous mountains in the Alps.

Blatten, in the Lötschental valley of southern Switzerland, had been home to about 300 people. Yet almost all of them were safe. Days earlier, experts had warned that the glacier was becoming unstable, and on 19 May the authorities decided to evacuate the whole village, including all its farm animals. One man, aged 64, was reported missing after the collapse. The village's mayor, Matthias Bellwald, summed up the feeling of the community in a few words: they had lost their village.

How did the experts know the danger was coming? The answer lies in careful observation. The story began with the mountain above the glacier, not the glacier itself. Weeks before the collapse, scientists noticed that the rock face above the Birch Glacier was becoming unstable. Loose rocks kept falling onto the glacier below. Over time, an estimated nine million tonnes of rock piled up on the ice.

This heavy load changed how the glacier behaved. Glaciers always move slowly downhill, but the extra weight pushed the Birch Glacier faster and faster. The authorities measured its speed rising from about 0.8 metres per day to between 1.5 and 2 metres per day. According to one report, it later moved as fast as 10 metres per day. In the final two days, smaller masses of ice and rock began to fall into the valley. Then, on 28 May, most of the glacier collapsed. Raphael Mayoraz, head of natural hazards for the Valais region, said it was the worst of the scenarios the experts had considered. the disaster did not end there. The debris blocked the Lonza River, which runs through the valley. Water began to build up behind the debris, forming a lake that flooded the buildings that had not been buried. To reduce the risk of flooding further down the valley, the authorities partly emptied a reservoir about six kilometres away.

Was climate change to blame? Scientists are cautious. Some experts link the collapse to the thawing of permafrost, ground in high mountains that normally stays frozen all year and helps hold rock together. As temperatures rise, this frozen ground can weaken. However, reports on the event describe the exact role of climate change as uncertain, while noting that rising temperatures in the region are thought to have been one factor.

The disaster is a sad story, but it also shows the value of science and early warning. Because experts watched the mountain closely and the authorities acted in time, a village was lost, but hundreds of lives were saved. As glaciers and mountains change in a warming world, this kind of careful monitoring may become more and more important.

passages.title: How Can a Fake Signal Fool GPS?
paragraphs: Every day in 2025, around a thousand aircraft around the world were affected by false navigation signals, according to researchers who track the problem. In some regions, pilots saw their screens suddenly show the plane in the wrong place, sometimes kilometres away from where it really was. Raphael Monstein, a researcher who maps these incidents, said that anyone flying out of Tel Aviv was practically certain to face spoofing. This is called GPS spoofing, and it has become a growing concern for aviation and shipping.

To understand spoofing, we first need to understand how GPS works. GPS, the Global Positioning System, uses satellites orbiting about 20,000 kilometres above the Earth. Each satellite constantly sends out a radio signal that includes the exact time and its own position. A GPS receiver, such as the one in your phone or in a plane, listens to signals from several satellites at once. By comparing how long each signal took to arrive, it can calculate its own location. There is a weakness in this system. By the time the signals travel 20,000 kilometres, they are extremely weak, far weaker than the signal from a mobile phone. This makes them easy to disturb in two ways.

The first is jamming. A jammer simply sends out strong radio noise on the same frequency, drowning out the real signals. The receiver loses its position completely. According to one report, a device the size of a cigarette packet can block GPS across several kilometres, and electronics costing only a few hundred euros are enough to disturb planes. Other satellite navigation systems, such as Europe's Galileo and China's BeiDou, face the same weakness.

The second, spoofing, is more cunning. A spoofer sends out fake signals that mimic the real ones, with the correct format and timing, but with false position information. Because the fake signals are slightly stronger than the real ones, the receiver locks on to them instead. The attacker can then slowly shift the calculated position, dragging the receiver towards any location. Ships in the Black Sea, for example, have reported their positions suddenly appearing at inland airports. Some ship captains even manipulate their own position transmitters to hide illegal fishing.

The problem has grown quickly. According to figures from the International Air Transport Association's 2025 safety report, GPS jamming rose by 67 percent between 2023 and 2025, while spoofing rose by 193 percent. The worst-affected regions include the Eastern Mediterranean, the Middle East, the Baltic region, and the Black Sea, many of them close to areas of military conflict.

Does this mean planes are in danger of crashing? Pilots do not rely on GPS alone. Aircraft also use inertial navigation, in which sensors measure every movement and acceleration to calculate the position, and radio navigation, which measures the distance to stations on the ground. Still, false signals can confuse systems and add stress to pilots' work.

The lesson reaches beyond planes. Many services we use daily, from map apps to delivery tracking, depend on GPS. Knowing that a signal can be faked reminds us that technology is only as trustworthy as the information it receives.

passages.title: Is Coffee Bad for an Irregular Heartbeat?
paragraphs: For decades, doctors have often told people with a common heart rhythm problem to cut down on coffee. The reasoning seemed simple. Caffeine can make the heart beat faster, so it might also trigger an irregular heartbeat. In November 2025, a clinical trial called DECAF put that advice to the test, and the result surprised many experts.

The condition studied was atrial fibrillation, often called AFib. It is the most common long-lasting heart rhythm disorder. In AFib, the upper chambers of the heart beat quickly and irregularly, which can increase the risk of stroke and heart failure. One treatment is cardioversion, a procedure that uses a controlled electric shock to return the heart to a normal rhythm. However, AFib often comes back afterwards.

The trial was led by researchers from the University of California, San Francisco, and the University of Adelaide in Australia, and was published in the journal JAMA. It involved 200 adults with persistent AFib who were already regular coffee drinkers and had undergone cardioversion. They were randomly divided into two groups. One group drank at least one cup of caffeinated coffee or one espresso each day. The other group was asked to abstain from coffee and all other caffeine for six months. The trial took place in five hospitals in the United States, Canada, and Australia. The participants' average age was 69, and most of them were men.

The results challenged the old assumption. Over six months, AFib returned in 47 percent of the coffee group and 64 percent of the no-caffeine group, a difference of 17 percentage points. The trial found no difference in harmful side effects between the groups. First author Christopher Wong called the results astounding.

On average, the coffee group drank about seven cups a week. Why might coffee help rather than harm? The researchers did not test this directly, but they suggested several possible explanations. First, coffee may encourage people to be more physically active, and exercise is known to reduce AFib. Second, caffeine blocks a natural substance in the body called adenosine, which can make AFib more likely. Third, coffee contains ingredients that reduce inflammation, a known risk factor for AFib. Caffeine also makes the body lose more water, which could slightly lower blood pressure. Finally, people who drink coffee may simply drink fewer unhealthy beverages. Each explanation is possible, and more than one may be true at the same time.

The trial also had clear limits. Participants knew which group they were in. Not everyone followed the rules perfectly: only 69 percent of the no-coffee group avoided coffee completely. The study was also fairly small, and it included only people who already drank about one cup a day. The results may not apply to people who drink much more coffee or who use energy drinks. the researchers argued that their results call into question routine advice to stop coffee among patients like those in the trial. They did not establish that coffee prevents every heart rhythm problem or that the findings apply to all patients. The case shows why long-standing medical assumptions need careful testing.

passages.title: What Does France's Deepest Shipwreck Tell Us?
paragraphs: On 4 March 2025, an underwater drone belonging to the French Navy was carrying out a routine survey of the seabed off Ramatuelle, near Saint-Tropez in southern France. The drone was part of a government project to explore and monitor France's deep-sea environment, from minerals to undersea internet cables. It was not looking for history. But its sonar detected something large on the seabed.

According to deputy maritime prefect Thierry de la Burgade, the sonar picked up something quite big. The team went back with a camera, and then again with a remote-controlled underwater robot to take clearer pictures. The work was carried out by the Navy's specialist deep-sea team, known as CEPHISMER. What they found was a wooden merchant ship lying 2,567 metres below the surface of the Mediterranean Sea. Arnaud Schaumasse, head of the French culture ministry's underwater archaeology department, announced in June 2025 that it was the deepest shipwreck ever found in French territorial waters. The archaeologists named it Camarat 4.

How can experts estimate a shipwreck's age and trading connections without bringing it to the surface? The answer is in its cargo. The wreck is about 30 metres long and 7 metres wide, which suggests it was a large vessel for its time, and it is surrounded by around 200 ceramic jugs with pinched spouts, as well as about 100 yellow plates. Many jugs are decorated with floral and geometric patterns. Some are marked with the letters IHS, a symbol made from the first three letters of the name of Jesus in Greek. These styles are typical of pottery made in Liguria, a region of northern Italy, in the 16th century. From this evidence, the archaeologists concluded that the ship was probably sailing from northern Italy about 500 years ago. The wreck also contains metal bars, two cooking pots, an anchor, and six cannons.

Why is the site so special? Wrecks that people can reach more easily are at risk of being looted, when objects are taken away to keep or sell. Camarat 4 is different. According to archaeologist Marine Sadania, its great depth has prevented anyone from recovering or looting objects, so the site has remained intact, as if time had stopped. For archaeologists, this is rare and valuable, because the position of every object can tell them how the ship was loaded and how it sank.

The deep sea is not completely untouched, however. The team noticed some modern household rubbish scattered among the old cargo, a reminder of how far human waste can travel. t he discovery also shows how technology is changing archaeology. The wreck lies far below the depths conventional divers can reach. Remotely operated robots and drones made it possible to survey the site and record its cargo.

The archaeologists described the cargo as remarkably well preserved after five centuries. Camarat 4 is a small window into 16th-century Mediterranean trade, when merchant ships carried everyday goods such as jugs and plates between busy ports. It reminds us that history is not only found in grand palaces and famous battles, but also on the quiet seabed, waiting to be found.

passages.title: How Did the Zipper Become Reliable?
paragraphs: Buttons have been used for thousands of years, while the modern zipper is little more than a century old. Its simple appearance hides a long history of experimentation. About twenty years separated Judson's unreliable device from Sundback's successful redesign, showing how inventions often develop through repeated improvement.

The first attempt came in 1851, when the American inventor Elias Howe, famous for his sewing machine, patented an idea he called an automatic, continuous clothing closure. It was never produced or sold.

More than forty years later, in 1893, a Chicago engineer named Whitcomb Judson showed a device called the clasp locker at the World's Columbian Exposition, a large world fair in Chicago. It was meant to replace the slow job of fastening tall boots. The clasp locker used a row of hooks on one side and a row of eyes on the other. A slider moved along the rows and joined the hooks and eyes together, so the user did not have to fasten each one by hand. The idea was clever, but the device worked badly. It jammed, it sprang open at the worst moments, and its metal parts tended to rust. It was also expensive. Almost nobody bought it.

The breakthrough came from Gideon Sundback, a Swedish-American electrical engineer who worked for Judson's company. By the end of 1913, he had redesigned the fastener from the beginning. He threw away the hooks and eyes completely and replaced them with rows of small, identical teeth. Each tooth had a tiny bump on one side and a hollow on the other. He also increased the number of fastening parts from about four per inch to about ten per inch.

This is how a modern zipper works. The slider is shaped like the letter Y. As you pull it up, it guides the two rows of teeth together at an angle, so that each tooth fits into the space between two teeth on the opposite side. The bump of one tooth sits inside the hollow of the next, and the teeth interlock tightly. Pulling the slider down does the opposite: it pushes the teeth apart. Because the teeth hold each other on all sides, the closed zipper resists being pulled apart, unlike the old hooks and eyes.

Sundback received a patent in 1917 for what he called a separable fastener. A similar device had been patented in Europe in 1911, but it was apparently never made. Just as importantly, he designed the machines needed to make it cheaply and reliably. In the same year, the United States Navy used the new fasteners on flying suits.

Interestingly, Sundback never called his invention a zipper. The name came in 1923 from the B.F. Goodrich Company, which used the fastener on rubber boots. The company liked the sound it made and named the boots Zippers. The name stuck. During the late 1920s and 1930s, zippers spread to clothing for men and women.

The zipper's history shows a lesson that applies to many technologies. A good idea is only the beginning. It often takes years of redesign, better materials, and better machines before an invention becomes something ordinary people can use every day.

passages.title: How Did a Greek Scholar Measure the Earth with a Shadow?
paragraphs: More than two thousand years ago, a scholar in the Egyptian city of Alexandria worked out how big the Earth was. He had no satellites, no aeroplanes, and no telescopes. He used a stick, a shadow, a known distance, and some careful thinking. His name was Eratosthenes, and his method is still taught in schools today because it shows how much can be learned from simple observations.

Eratosthenes worked at the great Library of Alexandria in the 3rd century BC. There, he learned about something unusual that happened every year in Syene, a town far to the south, now called Aswan. At noon on the summer solstice, the longest day of the year, the Sun was directly overhead in Syene. Upright objects cast no shadow, and sunlight shone straight down to the bottom of a deep well.

Eratosthenes realised that on the same day, at the same time, the Sun was not directly overhead in Alexandria. An upright stick there still cast a small shadow. He measured that shadow and used geometry to find the angle of the Sun's rays. The angle was about 7.2 degrees.

This is where his reasoning became brilliant. He assumed two things. First, the Earth is a sphere. Second, the Sun is so far away that its rays reach the Earth as nearly parallel lines. If both were true, then the difference in the shadows could only be caused by the curve of the Earth. The angle of 7.2 degrees in Alexandria would therefore be the same as the angle between Alexandria and Syene measured from the centre of the Earth.

A full circle has 360 degrees, and 7.2 degrees is exactly one fiftieth of that. So the distance between the two cities must be one fiftieth of the whole way around the Earth. According to the records, that distance was about 5,000 stadia. The stadion was an ancient unit of length. Eratosthenes simply multiplied: 5,000 times 50 equals 250,000 stadia. That was his estimate of the Earth's circumference, the distance all the way around it.

How accurate was he? The answer depends on the length of the stadion he used, which historians still do not know for certain. If he used a stadion of about 157.5 metres, his result would be about 39,375 kilometres, very close to the modern figure of about 40,075 kilometres at the equator. If he used a longer stadion, his answer could be about 15 percent too large. Either way, it was a remarkable achievement.

His method also had small weaknesses. Syene was not exactly south of Alexandria, and the distance between the cities was only an estimate, perhaps measured by trained people who counted their steps. Yet these errors did not change the main idea.

The most important lesson is the method itself. Eratosthenes combined an observation, two clear assumptions, and basic geometry to measure something far too large to measure directly. Scientists still use the same kind of thinking today. When you cannot measure something directly, you can often work it out from something smaller that you can measure.

passages.title: Why Does a Cut Apple Turn Brown?
paragraphs: Have you ever sliced an apple, left it on a plate for a few minutes, and come back to find it turning brown? The same thing happens to bananas, avocados, pears, and potatoes. Many people think the fruit is starting to rot. In fact, it is something different: a chemical reaction called enzymatic browning. Browning alone does not mean the fruit has spoiled.

To understand the reaction, we need to look inside the fruit's cells. An apple cell contains natural chemicals called polyphenols. It also contains an enzyme called polyphenol oxidase, or PPO. An enzyme is a substance that starts or speeds up a chemical reaction. In a whole, healthy apple, the polyphenols and the PPO are kept apart, stored in separate parts of the cell. Each compartment keeps its contents away from the other, so the reaction cannot happen.

Cutting, biting, or bruising the apple changes everything. The knife breaks the cell walls, and the polyphenols and PPO meet each other. Oxygen from the air also rushes in. Now the reaction can begin. With the help of oxygen, PPO changes the polyphenols into new chemicals called quinones. The quinones then join together into larger molecules, forming brown pigments similar to melanin, the pigment that colours human skin and hair.
Once you know that the reaction needs three things, the enzyme, the polyphenols, and oxygen, you can understand how to slow it down. You simply have to block one of them.

The most familiar trick is to coat the apple slices with lemon juice. Lemons contain ascorbic acid, also known as vitamin C, which acts as an antioxidant and delays the formation of brown pigments. Lemon juice is also acidic, and PPO works less well in strongly acidic conditions. The protection is temporary: once the antioxidant is used up, browning can resume. Other methods include covering the fruit to limit contact with air or heating it enough to deactivate the enzyme. Coating slices in syrup also makes it harder for oxygen to reach the fruit. Cooks often put cut potatoes or apples in water for the same reason.

Nearly all plant tissues contain PPO, which is why so many fruits and vegetables behave in the same way. Some fruits brown faster than others, because the amount of PPO and polyphenols differs between varieties and depends on growing conditions. Scientists have used this knowledge. The Arctic apple, developed by a Canadian company, has had its PPO genes switched off, so it does not brown even when it is cut or bruised. It went on sale in some shops in the United States in 2017.

Enzymatic browning is not always unwanted. The same type of reaction helps create the colours and flavours of tea, coffee, and chocolate. Whether browning is good or bad depends on what we want from our food.
The next time you prepare fruit, you can use this knowledge like a scientist. Ask yourself which ingredient of the reaction you can remove, and choose your method from there.
